2.title: Reproduce

3.text:
A server commits rows to a Merkle root and sends one row plus its proof to a client. The client
holds only the trusted root. Edit the rows, pick one to prove, then change the claimed value to
see tampering rejected. The browser mirrors BinaryMerkleTree<Sha256> with WebCrypto: leaves are
SHA-256(0x00 ‖ row), internal nodes SHA-256(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right), and the leaf layer is padded
to a power of two with Sha256::empty(). Roots match the Rust crate for the same rows.

25.text:
MerkleForge is a Rust framework for authenticated data structures. You put data in, get a
32-byte root out, and hand out small proofs that anyone holding the root can check, without
downloading the rest of the data.
25.title: Why MerkleForge

26.text:
Data verification is one of the major bottlenecks in modern blockchain networks. As systems
process millions of transactions, checking the integrity of state data gets slow and
resource-intensive. Every state lookup, transaction batch, and light-client proof depends on the
speed and correctness of the underlying data structure. The Rust ecosystem has strong cryptographic building blocks, but Merkle tree support is spread
across variant-specific crates. Libraries like rs-merkle focus on binary trees, while
Ethereum-specific tries are maintained separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with
different APIs, documentation depth, test coverage, and benchmark methodology.
26.title: The problem

27.text:
MerkleForge unifies the three Merkle tree variants used across production systems behind one
API: VariantTypical useBinaryMerkleTree<H>Transaction batching, Bitcoin-style SPV, logs, file chunksSparseMerkleTree<H>Account state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollupsMerklePatriciaTrie<H>Ethereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses All three are generic over a HashFunction, implement the shared
MerkleTree<H> trait, and produce proofs that verify statelessly.
27.title: The solution

28.text:
Unified API. BinaryMerkleTree<H>, SparseMerkleTree<H>, and MerklePatriciaTrie<H> all
implement MerkleTree<H>, so generic code works with any of them.Pluggable hash functions. Swap SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 by changing one type
parameter. Generics are monomorphised at compile time, so there is no runtime dispatch.Stateless verification. A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
the leaf bytes. See Proofs & stateless verification.Domain separation built in. Leaves hash as H(0x00 ‖ data) and internal nodes as
H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right), which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the
mental model.Reproducible benchmarks. A dedicated Criterion suite compares hashes, tree variants, and
other Rust Merkle libraries. See Benchmarks.Tested. Unit, integration, property-based (Proptest), and Ethereum test-vector tests.#![forbid(unsafe_code)] in every published crate.

30.title: Next steps

31.text:
Think of a Merkle root as a fingerprint for many values. Change any value and the fingerprint
changes. A proof is the short path that lets another machine check one value against that
fingerprint.
31.title: Mental model

32.text:
PieceWhat it isIn MerkleForgeLeafThe hash of one value you inserted.H::hash(data), computed for you by insert.RootOne digest that commits to every leaf.tree.root() returns Option<&H::Digest>.ProofThe sibling hashes on the path from one leaf to the root.MerkleProof<D> (binary), SparseMerkleProof<D>, MptProof<D>.VerifierCode that rebuilds the root from a leaf and a proof.ProofVerifier::verify and the per-tree verify* functions.                  root = H(0x01 ‖ n01 ‖ n23)
                /                          \
     n01 = H(0x01 ‖ l0 ‖ l1)      n23 = H(0x01 ‖ l2 ‖ l3)
        /            \               /            \
 l0 = H(0x00‖a)  l1 = H(0x00‖b)  l2 = H(0x00‖c)  l3 = H(0x00‖d) To prove a is leaf 0, the prover sends l1 and n23. The verifier computes l0 from a, then
n01, then the root, and compares it with the root it already trusts. For n leaves that is
⌈log₂ n⌉ hashes, no matter how big the dataset is.
32.title: The four pieces

33.text:
The prover (a server, indexer, or full node) holds the full tree. It publishes the root and
answers proof requests.The verifier (a light client, browser, contract, or embedded device) holds only a trusted
root, for example from a block header or a signed checkpoint. A proof is only as good as the root you check it against. Get the root from a source you trust.
33.title: Who holds what

34.text:
MerkleForge hashes leaves and internal nodes in different domains: HashPre-imageLeafH(0x00 ‖ data)Internal nodeH(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right) Without the prefixes, an internal node's pre-image (left ‖ right, 64 bytes) is also a valid leaf
value. An attacker could then present an internal node as if it were a leaf and forge a "proof"
for data that was never inserted. This is a second-preimage attack. With distinct prefixes, a
leaf hash can never equal an internal node hash for a different structure. The Sha256 and Keccak256 adapters use the byte prefixes above. Blake3 gets the same
separation from BLAKE3's derive_key mode with two context strings. See
Hash functions for the exact constructions.
34.title: Domain separation: 0x00 and 0x01

35.title: Verifying by hand

36.text:
BinaryMerkleTree pads the leaf layer to the next power of two with H::empty(), the hash of an
empty leaf. Five leaves become eight slots.SparseMerkleTree has 2²⁵⁶ slots and precomputes the root of an empty subtree at every level,
so empty regions cost nothing to store.MerklePatriciaTrie follows Ethereum's node layout and has no padding. Because empty slots hash to H::empty(), empty leaf data is rejected with
MerkleError::EmptyLeafData; otherwise an inserted empty value would be indistinguishable from
padding.
36.title: Padding and empty slots

37.text:
MerkleProof::leaf_count tells the verifier how deep the path should be. The root does not
commit to it, so any count with the same padded size verifies. If the exact number of leaves matters
to you, get it from a trusted source and compare.
37.title: One caveat: leaf_count is not committed

57.text:
Correctness and performance fixes. Roots and proofs for the shipped hash adapters are unchanged. Added: BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves (one-pass O(n) build),
SparseMerkleTree::verify_membership (checks the proof's key),
HashFunction::hash_encoded_node, NodeEntry::commitment, and Clone / Debug / Serialize /
Deserialize for all three trees.Fixed: sparse and Patricia inserts and removals recompute only the changed path (4,000
sparse inserts: about 223 s to 0.2 s; one sparse proof: 151 ms to 25 µs; 4,000 Patricia inserts:
about 5.9 s to 0.02 s). MerkleTree::insert on sparse and Patricia trees no longer overwrites a
leaf after a removal.Breaking: the default HashFunction::hash_nodes now hashes 0x01 ‖ left ‖ right;
MerklePatriciaTrie selects plain Keccak through hash_encoded_node instead of the algorithm
name; the hidden MptNode::__DigestMarker variant is gone.Deprecated: SparseMerkleTree::verify. Use verify_membership.

63.title: Design properties

64.text:
Trust the root, not the prover. A proof shows consistency with a root; it says nothing about
whether that root is the right one.MerkleProof::leaf_count is not committed by the binary root. Obtain it independently if it
matters.Check the key on sparse proofs with verify_membership. The deprecated
SparseMerkleTree::verify accepts a valid proof for any key holding the value.Canonical leaf encoding. Prover and verifier must hash exactly the same bytes.Custom hash adapters must keep leaf and node domains separate. Since Unreleased, the default
hash_nodes applies the 0x01 prefix for you. See
Hash functions.
64.title: What integrators must get right

65.text:
MerkleForge uses Criterion benchmarks in the unpublished
merkle-bench crate to compare hash adapters, tree variants, proof generation, proof
verification, and other Rust Merkle libraries. Criterion reports mean, median, and standard
deviation to filter out noise. Lower latency is better; higher throughput is better. For the latest CI numbers with links to every
Criterion report, see the live benchmark explorer. The tables below are copied from BENCHMARKS.md
(run date 2026-08-17). That run predates the Unreleased sparse-tree and Patricia-trie
performance fixes, which cut 4,000 sequential sparse inserts from about 223 s to 0.2 s and
4,000 Patricia inserts from about 5.9 s to 0.02 s. Sparse and Patricia numbers here are therefore
pessimistic. Cells marked not captured were not completed in that run.

80.text:
The default energy workload builds a 100,000-leaf binary tree with SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3.
Criterion measures wall-clock time; Linux perf collects CPU package energy externally. cargo bench --bench bench_energy   # wall clock → target/criterion/bench_energy/
80.title: Energy

81.text:
On Intel and some AMD machines the kernel exposes RAPL counters through the power/* PMU. Check
support, then run the helper script: perf list 'power/energy-*'
./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy The script collects power/energy-pkg/ (package Joules), power/energy-cores/ and
power/energy-ram/ when available, cycles, instructions, cache-references, cache-misses,
and duration_time. Some machines need elevated privileges: sudo ./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy
# or
sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=0 Use the privileged path only on a machine you control. The explicit command behind the script: sudo perf stat -a -r 3 \
  -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,duration_time,power/energy-pkg/ \
  -- cargo bench --bench bench_energy -a records across all CPUs, which matters because package energy is a socket-level reading.
81.title: RAPL counters with perf

82.text:
If perf doesn't show power/energy-pkg/, try turbostat: sudo turbostat --Summary --Joules --out profiling/turbostat-energy.txt -- \
  cargo bench --bench bench_energy powertop is less precise but can capture a repeatable system-level profile while the benchmark
runs in another terminal: sudo powertop --time=60 --html=profiling/powertop-energy.html
82.title: Fallbacks

83.text:
Lower elapsed time: construction finished sooner.Lower power/energy-pkg/ Joules: the CPU package used less energy.Fewer cycles for the same workload: less CPU work.Cache misses explain why runs with similar hash speed differ in time or energy. Energy measurements are hardware-specific. Report the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version,
and command line with every table. BLAKE3's lower cycles per byte usually means less energy per
proof, which is why the suite measures all three algorithms. The full guide lives in
benchmarks/ENERGY.md
and profiling/README.md.

84.text:
BinaryMerkleTree<H> is a balanced binary tree over an ordered list of leaves. It stores leaves
and internal nodes in one flat, cache-friendly array, pads the leaf layer to a power of two, and
gives O(log n) inclusion proofs addressed by LeafIndex. Use it for transaction batches, logs, file chunks, snapshot commitments, and Bitcoin-style SPV.

BinaryMerkleTree implements Clone, Debug, Default, Serialize, and Deserialize. The
serialized form stores only the hash algorithm name and the leaf hashes; internal nodes are

92.text:
MerkleForge ships three tree variants. They share the MerkleTree<H> trait but are built for
different shapes of data. BinaryMerkleTree<H>SparseMerkleTree<H>MerklePatriciaTrie<H>Data shapeOrdered listMap from 32-byte keys to valuesMap from byte keys to valuesAddressed byLeafIndex[u8; 32] key&[u8] keyProofsInclusionMembership and non-membershipMembership and non-membership (RLP witness)Proof size⌈log₂ n⌉ siblings256 siblings, empty ones compressed to NoneOne RLP node per trie level on the pathBest hashSha256 or Blake3Sha256 or Blake3Keccak256 for Ethereum rootsTypical useTransaction batches, logs, file chunks, SPVAccount state, rollups, allowlistsEthereum state, receipts, storage proofs
92.title: Choosing a tree

93.text:
You have a list and prove items by position: use
BinaryMerkleTree. It has the smallest proofs and the fastest
construction.You have a key-value map and need to prove a key is absent: use
SparseMerkleTree. Keys are 32 bytes, so hash longer keys
first.You need roots or witnesses that Ethereum tooling understands: use
MerklePatriciaTrie<Keccak256>.

94.title: Writing code that works with any variant

95.text:
Binary: insert appends and returns the next LeafIndex. remove replaces the leaf with
H::empty(); later indices are unchanged.Sparse: leaf index i is stored at a key whose last 8 bytes are i in big-endian order.
insert returns the first unoccupied index at or above the leaf count, so it never overwrites a
leaf after a removal. generate_proof returns a MerkleProof with 256 path nodes.Patricia: leaf index i is stored under the key b"merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:" ‖ i
(8 bytes, big-endian). generate_proof through the trait returns
MerkleError::UnsupportedOperation, because Patricia proofs are key-addressed. Use
MerklePatriciaTrie::generate_proof(key) instead. Use the trait for generic plumbing (ingestion, metadata, benchmarks). Use each variant's native API
when you need key-addressed proofs.
95.title: How the trait maps onto each variant

96.text:
Every fallible MerkleForge API returns Result<T, MerkleError>. Verification functions return
bool instead: a bad proof is an expected outcome, not an error. MerkleError lives in merkle_core::error (and the prelude). It implements Debug, Clone,
PartialEq, Eq, Display, and, with the default std feature, std::error::Error, so it works
with ?, Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, and thiserror.

97.text: VariantRaised whenEmptyTreeProof generation (or binary remove) on a tree with no leavesIndexOutOfBounds { index, len }A LeafIndex past the last logical leafInvalidProofAvailable to APIs that report failed verification as an error (the shipped verifiers return false instead)InvalidProofStructure(String)A proof's shape is inconsistent (e.g. sparse proof generation with a non-256 depth)EmptyLeafDataInserting an empty value (empty data would be indistinguishable from padding)SerializationError(String)to_bytes failedDeserializationError(String)from_bytes got malformed dataHashError(String)An internal hashing step failed (for custom adapters; not raised by the shipped ones)UnsupportedOperation(&'static str)The variant can't do this, e.g. removing a missing sparse or Patricia key, or index-based Patricia proofsRlpError(String)Malformed RLP or hex-prefix data in the Patricia trie

101.text:
Every MerkleForge tree is generic over H: HashFunction. The hash decides the digest type, how
leaves and internal nodes are hashed, and what an empty slot looks like. Swapping it is a
type-level change: Rust monomorphises the generics, so there is no runtime dispatch.

Ethereum interop: Keccak256. Required for Patricia roots that match Ethereum.Broad interoperability: Sha256. Ubiquitous, and fast on CPUs with SHA extensions.Raw speed: Blake3. In the published run it hashed 1 MB at 5.99 GiB/s versus 1.28 GiB/s for
SHA-256 and 291 MiB/s for Keccak-256. See Benchmarks. A tree built with one hash can't be read with another: serialized trees store the algorithm
name and deserialization rejects a mismatch.

107.text:
MerklePatriciaTrie<H> implements Ethereum's Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT): nibble-addressed byte
keys, four node types (empty, leaf, extension, branch), hex-prefix path encoding, RLP-encoded
nodes, and Ethereum's inline-or-hash node references. With Keccak256, roots match Ethereum: the implementation is tested against the official
trietest.json and trieanyorder.json vectors from the Ethereum test suite.

merkle-core, the crate with the traits, proof types, and errors, supports no_std targets with
a global allocator. That lets embedded devices, enclaves, and WebAssembly modules share proof types
with your servers and implement their own verifiers.

118.text:
Everything in merkle-core: HashFunction, MerkleTree, ProofVerifier, Serializable
(bincode), MerkleProof, ProofNode, ProofSide, LeafIndex, NodeIndex, TreeMetadata, and
MerkleError (without the std::error::Error impl). merkleforge-hash and merkle-variants currently depend on merkle-core with default features
and use std (the sparse tree uses std::collections::HashMap), so they are std-only. On a
no_std target, depend on merkle-core alone and supply a HashFunction adapter and verifier.

119.title: A no_std verifier

120.text:
A MerkleForge proof lets a verifier check one value against a trusted root, with no access to the
tree. This is the property that makes Merkle trees useful for light clients, bridges, browsers, and
embedded devices.
120.title: Proofs & stateless verification

121.title: Proof types

122.text:
1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf_data)
2. for each node in proof.path:
     if node.side == Left:  current = H(0x01 ‖ node.hash ‖ current)
     if node.side == Right: current = H(0x01 ‖ current ‖ node.hash)
3. return current == expected_root BinaryMerkleTree::verify also rejects proofs whose structure is inconsistent: empty leaf data,
leaf_index >= leaf_count, a path length that doesn't match the padded size, or sides that don't
match the bits of leaf_index. It returns false and never panics on malformed input.
122.title: The verification algorithm

125.text:
The root. A proof only shows that a leaf is consistent with some root. Get the root from a
trusted source: a block header, a signed checkpoint, a contract.The leaf encoding. Verify the exact bytes that were inserted. Agree on a canonical encoding
(field order, separators, number formats) between prover and verifier.Not leaf_count. The binary root doesn't commit to MerkleProof::leaf_count. If the number
of leaves matters, obtain it independently.The key, for sparse proofs. Use verify_membership, which checks the proof's key. The
deprecated SparseMerkleTree::verify does not.

leaf count. See Serialization for encoding options.

132.text:
TreeMetadata implements Serialize and Deserialize, but its string fields are
&'static str, so it can't be deserialized from an owned buffer and is not Serializable.
Serialize it for logs and dashboards, for example with serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata()).
See Metadata.
132.title: Metadata

133.text:
SparseMerkleTree<H> models a fixed-depth 256-bit key space: 2²⁵⁶ leaf slots, almost all
empty. It stores only non-empty nodes, precomputes the empty-subtree hash at every level, and
compresses single-leaf subtrees into shortcut nodes (Buterin, 2018) and small subtrees into batch
entries (Ouvrard, 2018/2019). Use it for account state, key-value commitments, allowlists, and rollup state, especially when you
must prove that a key is absent.

nodes. Prefer the key-addressed API above for real state.
